messages.subject: Re: Surveys which combine both point and line transects
messages.subject_clean: Surveys which combine both point and line transects
messages.body_plain:
Nicole-

Transit speed can affect detection probability and you can use it as a
covariate for it.  I have a recent ms on this in regard to aircraft
speed in Wildlife Research.  However, with marine mammals you have the
added complication that vessel speed also affects the probability that
the critter is available at the surface.  This aspect will not be
handled using vessel speed as a covariate because it will affect g(0)
which is not incorporated into DISTANCE.

I would not recommend treating your data as a point transect unless what
you have is cue counting data.

regards --jeff

Nicole Koshure wrote:
> > I am currently working on a dataset of opportunistic distance sightings from
> > a marine mammal monitoring program. My aim is to create a Generalized
> > Additive Model which will allow me to predict density and distribution of
> > cetaceans within my study area. Because the vessel both travels through the
> > study area and spends time monitoring vessel activity around killer whales
> > there are times when the vessel is traveling at different speeds. I can
> > determine when the vessel was monitoring and when they were transiting. As
> > such, I wondered if it made sense to analyze the sightings collected when
> > monitoring (travelling at less than 5 knots) as point transects in Distance
> > and when the vessel is transiting to analyze them as line transects. The
> > difficulty with this is that I am not sure how this will affect how I build
> > the model as I will have different detection functions depending on what the
> > vessel is doing?
> >
> > I was also wondering if one way to tackle this issue would be to use vessel
> > speed as a covariate in the MCDS function of Distance - or if that is at all
> > appropriate.
> >
> > Any thoughts on this would be much appreciated.
> >
> > Thank You
> > Nicole
> >
> >

--

messages.subject: Help with square transect survey design in DISTANCE 5.0
messages.subject_clean: Help with square transect survey design in DISTANCE 5.0
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm currently planning distance sampling surveys for ungulates and green
peafowl within predominately dry forest habitat in eastern Cambodia. I plan
to use 3.2 km long square transects (800m each side) and hope to use the
survey design function within DISTANCE 5.0 to design the survey (i.e. plot
the location of the transects and ensure survey design is suitable).

However DISTANCE 5.0 does not appear to have a function for designing square
transects. Would it be acceptable to use the simple random point sampling
option and use these points as start points of the square transects or would
the outputs on coverage probability be inaccurate?

Thanks

Tom Gray (WWF Cambodia).

--

If you have a large study area, that would be fine.  If the study area
is small, you'll need to give some thought to edge effects.  See Fig 7.3
of the 2001 intro to distance sampling book.  Chapter 7 of the 2004 book
considers edge effects in greater detail.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: post stratification of geograhically fragmented and desity varied
messages.subject_clean: post stratification of geograhically fragmented and desity varied
messages.body_plain:
Dear listers,

I'm looking for a little advice on how to treat some data that requires
post-stratification on account of a large variation in encounter rate over
several fragmented groups of the same species.

After systematically surveying the whole range of a species of tortoises it
came to light the whole population was now living in four geographically
isolated and fragmented groups. Three groups with low densities of objects;
a total of 22 objects detected over 33,  1km transects (detection rate
varied from 0-6 objects for km of transect). The remaining group, in the
smallest geographical area, however was very densely populated with 66
objects detected over 3 transects. Due to the fragmented nature of the local
habitat the transects in this last group were smaller in length (500m, 350m
and 150m respectively) than the three lowly populated groups (detection rate
of 66 objects for km of transect).

Without stratifying by geographical location as a covariate prior to
analyses the resulting density and abundance estimates exhibit low precision
(very large upper and lower CI). I'm thinking that stratifying the data by
geographical area (one stratum for the three low density groups and one
stratum for the high density group) could be the best way? However Buckland
et al, (Ch 3.7) advises against this; stating that post-stratification by
geographical location can result in overestimation for areas of high
encounter rate and underestimation for those areas of low encounter rate.

Does anyone have any ideas on how I can get around this problem and achieve
a reliable estimation of tortoise population and density across the now
fragmented range? Any help is much appreciated.

Thanks

Ryan

-----------------------------------------
Ryan Walker, MSc, MIEEM
+44(0)7739 740701

ry...@nautilusecology.org

--

messages.body_plain:
Distance sampling folks.  For a few years now, Tiago Marques has been
building an extensive and searchable list of distance sampling
references online, on his web site.  This valuable page has now moved
location, so update your bookmarks.  The new address is:

http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distancesamplingreferences/

Tiago welcomes suggestions for additional papers to add to the list -
his email address is at the bottom of the page.

Cheers,

  - Len Thomas
